title.en: Anthropometry and nutritional assessment in children

intro.en: Measuring growth, grading undernutrition, reading dehydration and deficiency signs, and screening for dysmorphism at the paediatric bedside.

title.en: Weight assessment and IAP grading of malnutrition

aka: IAP classification of protein energy malnutrition
items.summary: Weighing technique with age based expected weight rules, birth weight multiples, and the Indian Academy of Pediatrics percentage grading of protein energy malnutrition.

blocks.title: Expected weight rules
bullets: Low birth weight means a birth weight below 2.5 kg.
Below 1 year, expected weight in kg equals age in months plus 9, all divided by 2.
From 1 to 7 years, expected weight in kg equals age in years plus 4, all multiplied by 2.
From 7 to 12 years, expected weight in kg equals age in years multiplied by 3.
A 4 year old therefore has an expected weight of 16 kg by the middle rule.

blocks.title: Weight as multiples of birth weight
bullets: Weight doubles by 5 months and triples by 1 year.
It reaches 4 times by 2 years and 5 times by 3 years.
It reaches 6 times by 5 years, 7 times by 7 years and 10 times by 10 years.
A 1 year old born at 2.5 kg is thus expected to weigh 7.5 kg.

blocks.title: IAP grading by percentage of expected weight
Points to remember
bullets: The letter K is added after the grade when oedema is present, for example grade 2 with K.

viva.q: How do you work out the expected weight of a 4 year old?
viva.a: Use the 1 to 7 year rule: age plus 4, times 2, giving 16 kg for a 4 year old.

viva.q: What weight multiples of birth weight should a child reach at 1, 2 and 5 years?
viva.a: Three times by 1 year, 4 times by 2 years, and 6 times by 5 years.

viva.q: What does the K suffix mean in the IAP malnutrition grade?
viva.a: It records that oedema is present alongside the weight based grade.

image.brief: Infant spring weighing scale with sling beside an electronic standing scale for older children, both on a plain background, front three quarter view.

title.en: Length, height, short stature and parental target height

items.summary: Measuring recumbent length below 2 years and standing height above, milestone values, the height formula, short stature definition with causes, and target height from parental heights.

blocks.title: How to measure
bullets: Use an infantometer for recumbent length up to 2 years of age.
Use a stadiometer for standing height above 2 years of age.

blocks.title: Formula and growth multiples
bullets: From 2 to 12 years, height in cm equals age in years times 6, plus 77.
Height doubles by 4 years of age and triples by 13 years.

blocks.title: Short stature definition and causes
bullets: Short stature means height below the 3rd centile or over 2 standard deviations under the median for age and sex.
Proportionate causes include intrauterine growth restriction, undernutrition, chronic infection such as tuberculosis, and hormone deficits such as low thyroid, low growth hormone and excess cortisol.
Disproportionate causes include achondroplasia and vertebral defects such as Klippel Feil syndrome.

blocks.title: Mid parental height and predicted adult height
bullets: For a boy, add both parental heights in cm plus 13, then divide by 2.
For a girl, add both parental heights in cm minus 13, then divide by 2.
Predicted adult height lies within 2.5 cm on either side of that target.
A second estimate doubles the length measured at 2 years, again within 2.5 cm either way.

viva.q: When do you use an infantometer and when a stadiometer?
viva.a: An infantometer measures recumbent length up to 2 years; a stadiometer measures standing height above 2 years.

viva.q: How do you calculate the mid parental height for a girl?
viva.a: Add both parental heights in cm, subtract 13, divide by 2; adult height falls within 2.5 cm of it.

viva.q: Give one proportionate and one disproportionate cause of short stature.
viva.a: Chronic undernutrition or thyroid deficiency keeps proportions, while achondroplasia distorts them.

image.brief: Infantometer board with fixed head plate and sliding foot plate beside a wall mounted stadiometer, plain background, side view with centimetre markings visible.

title.en: Ponderal index, bone age and stunting classifications

items.summary: Index of body proportionality at birth, comparing bone age with height age, and charting chronic undernutrition by the Waterlow and World Health Organization systems.

blocks.title: Ponderal index at birth
bullets: The index equals weight in grams divided by the cube of length in cm, times 100.
Above 2.5 is normal, 2 to 2.5 means symmetric growth restriction, and below 2 means asymmetric growth restriction.

blocks.title: Bone age against height age
bullets: Bone age matches height age in constitutional delay and in simple undernutrition.
Bone age lags behind height age in growth hormone deficiency and in low thyroid states.

blocks.title: Waterlow height for age stunting grades

head: Measure
Moderate malnutrition
Severe malnutrition
rows: Between minus 3 and minus 2 standard deviation scores, about 70-79 percent.
Between minus 3 and minus 2 scores, about 85-89 percent.

head: Weight for height
Height for age
Reading
rows: Wasted and stunted, hence acute on chronic.

viva.q: How do you read the ponderal index in a newborn?
viva.a: Weight in grams over length cubed in cm, times 100: above 2.5 is normal, 2 to 2.5 symmetric restriction, below 2 asymmetric restriction.

viva.q: What does bone age lagging behind height age suggest?
viva.a: Growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism, while equal bone and height ages fit constitutional delay or simple undernutrition.

viva.q: How does the combined Waterlow chart separate acute from chronic undernutrition?
viva.a: Low weight for height alone means acute wasting, low height for age alone means chronic stunting, and both low means acute on chronic.

image.brief: Wall growth chart with centile curves beside a small table card of stunting and wasting cutoffs, plain clinic background, straight on view.

title.en: Kwashiorkor, marasmus and failure to thrive

items.summary: Bedside contrast of oedematous and wasted malnutrition across four grades, plus the growth chart definition of failure to thrive.

head: Grade
Kwashiorkor, weight 60-80 percent with oedema
Marasmus, weight below 60 percent without oedema
rows: Loose skin folds in armpit and groin.
Face turns rounded and moon like.
Loose folds over thigh and buttocks.
Swelling spreads to sacrum and abdominal wall.
Loose folds over chest and spine.
Fluid collects in the abdomen as ascites.
Loss of the buccal fat pad of the cheek.

blocks.title: Related definitions
bullets: Undernutrition means weight 60-80 percent of expected with no oedema.
Marasmic kwashiorkor means weight below 60 percent with oedema present.
Failure to thrive means weight for age below the 3rd centile, or a fall crossing two major centile lines within a short time.

viva.q: How do kwashiorkor and marasmus differ by weight and oedema?
viva.a: Kwashiorkor holds weight at 60-80 percent of expected with oedema; marasmus falls below 60 percent with no oedema and loose skin folds.

viva.q: What is marasmic kwashiorkor?
viva.a: Weight below 60 percent of expected together with oedema, blending both pictures.

viva.q: When is failure to thrive diagnosed on the growth chart?
viva.a: Weight for age below the 3rd centile, or a downward crossing of two major centile lines over a short period.

viva.q: How does grade 4 kwashiorkor differ from grade 1?
viva.a: Grade 1 shows only peripheral swelling, while grade 4 shows abdominal fluid collection as ascites.

image.brief: Side by side clinical illustrations of an oedematous malnourished child and a wasted child with loose skin folds, plain background, full body front view, no identifiers.

title.en: Head circumference, skull signs and small or large heads

items.summary: Tape measurement of head growth with milestone values, definitions of large and small heads with causes, and skull clues such as softening and frontal bossing.

blocks.title: Large and small head definitions
bullets: Macrocephaly means head circumference over 2 standard deviations above the median for age.
Causes include hydrocephalus, mucopolysaccharidosis, fragile X syndrome and intracranial tumours.
Microcephaly means head circumference over 3 standard deviations below the median for age.

groups.label: Primary
bullets: Familial patterns, chromosomal syndromes such as trisomy 5, 18 and 21, and brain malformations.

groups.label: Secondary
bullets: Maternal diabetes, meningitis, intrauterine TORCH infection, birth asphyxia, radiation, and drugs such as phenytoin and alcohol.

blocks.title: Working rules and skull signs
bullets: One standard deviation is about 2.5 percent of the expected head circumference; at 50 cm expected, 1 standard deviation is 1.25 cm.
Up to 1 year, head circumference for length equals length in cm divided by 2, within 2.5 cm either way.
Craniotabes means soft parchment like skull bones that dent like a ping pong ball, seen in rickets and excess vitamin A.
Frontal bossing is seen in rickets and in thalassaemia major.
About 90 percent of brain growth finishes within the first 2 years.

viva.q: How do macrocephaly and microcephaly cutoffs differ in this book?
viva.a: Macrocephaly lies over 2 standard deviations above the median, while microcephaly lies over 3 standard deviations below it.

viva.q: Name three secondary causes of microcephaly.
viva.a: Intrauterine TORCH infection, meningitis, and maternal diabetes, plus birth asphyxia, radiation, phenytoin or alcohol exposure.

viva.q: What is craniotabes and what causes it?
viva.a: Softened skull bones that indent like a ping pong ball, seen in rickets and vitamin A excess.

image.brief: Non stretchable tape passed around an infant head over brow and occiput, plain background, side view showing tape placement.

credit.author: Gaia Skin Naturals Australia; photographer not identified

unsure: Book defines microcephaly as over 3 standard deviations below the median while macrocephaly is over 2 above; kept as printed though the asymmetry is unusual.

title.en: Arm, body mass and chest circumference screening

items.summary: Mid arm tape grading for wasting, body mass index cutoffs for thinness and overweight, and chest growth against head size in infancy.

blocks.title: Mid upper arm circumference from 1 to 5 years
bullets: Measure midway between the acromion and the olecranon process.
Read the value on a Shakir tape and match its colour band.

blocks.title: Body mass index below 12 years
bullets: The index equals weight in kg divided by the square of height in metres.
Below 15 suggests undernutrition, above 22 overweight, and above 25 obesity.

blocks.title: Chest circumference against head size
bullets: Measure just below nipple level at mid inspiration.
At birth the head exceeds the chest; the two equalise around 9-12 months.
After 1 year the chest exceeds the head.

viva.q: Where and in whom is the mid arm circumference measured?
viva.a: Midway between acromion and olecranon, in children aged 1 to 5 years, read on a Shakir tape.

viva.q: What Shakir tape reading means severe wasting?
viva.a: Below 12.5 cm in the red band; 12.5-13.5 cm is moderate and 13.5-16.5 cm normal.

viva.q: When does the chest catch up with the head?
viva.a: The head is larger at birth, both match around 9-12 months, and the chest leads after 1 year.

image.brief: Shakir tricolour tape wrapped around the midpoint of a young child upper arm, plain background, close view showing green yellow and red bands.

title.en: Body proportions and surface area estimation

items.summary: Segment ratio milestones with infantile and advanced patterns, arm span behaviour with age, and weight band formulas for body surface area.

blocks.title: Upper to lower segment ratio by age
Reading abnormal ratios
bullets: An infantile high ratio is seen in achondroplasia, low thyroid states, rickets and early puberty.
An advanced low ratio is seen in Turner and Klinefelter syndromes, spinal tuberculosis, kyphoscoliosis and mucopolysaccharidosis.

blocks.title: Arm span behaviour
bullets: At birth the span is shorter than body length and matches height around 10 years.
The book notes the span stays short in Marfan syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, Klinefelter syndrome and homocystinuria.
Height exceeding span before 10 years points toward early puberty.

blocks.title: Body surface area by weight band

head: Weight band
Formula giving area in square metres

blocks.title: Spot values to remember
bullets: Surface area is 0.5 at 15 kg, 0.8 at 20 kg, 1 at 30 kg and 1.3 at 40 kg.

viva.q: What segment ratios do you expect at birth, 2 years and 9 years?
viva.a: 1.7:1 at birth, 1.5:1 at 2 years, and 1:1 at 9 years, falling to 0.9:1 after 10 years.

viva.q: How do you estimate body surface area for a 15 kg child?
viva.a: Using the 11-20 kg rule it works to about 0.5 square metres; spot values are 0.8 at 20, 1 at 30 and 1.3 at 40 kg.

viva.q: What does a high infantile segment ratio suggest?
viva.a: Achondroplasia, hypothyroidism, rickets or early puberty; a low advanced ratio suggests Turner or Klinefelter syndromes or spinal disease.

image.brief: Measuring tape stretched fingertip to fingertip across a standing child with arms out sideways, plain background, front view showing full span.

unsure: Book states arm span stays shorter than height in Marfan syndrome, kept as printed though standard teaching says the span exceeds height in Marfan; needs reviewer check.

title.en: Pallor, jaundice, cyanosis and clubbing signs

items.summary: Where to look for anaemia, jaundice and blue discolouration with laboratory cutoffs, plus the four grades of finger clubbing with its disease associations.

blocks.title: Pallor sites
bullets: Inspect the lower palpebral conjunctiva, tongue dorsum, palms, oral mucosa and nails.
Pale palm and sole creases allow a comment on severe pallor.

blocks.title: Jaundice sites and cutoff
bullets: Yellow staining of skin and mucosa becomes visible above a serum bilirubin of 2 mg per dl.
Examine the bulbar conjunctiva, tongue dorsum, palms and soles.

blocks.title: Cyanosis definition and distribution
bullets: Bluish skin and mucosa appear when reduced haemoglobin exceeds 5 grams per dl.
Look at lips, nail beds and ear lobes.
Central cyanosis colours mucosa and limbs together; peripheral cyanosis colours limbs only.

head: Grade
Nail finding
rows: Soft nail bed with extra fluctuation.
Lost nail bed angle past the normal 160 degrees, giving a positive Schamroth window test.
Bony overgrowth of hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.

blocks.title: Associations to remember
bullets: Clubbing follows congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, lung abscess, bronchiectasis and Crohn disease.
False clubbing from excess parathyroid activity is termed pseudoclubbing.

viva.q: Where do you look for pallor and when do you call it severe?
viva.a: Lower conjunctiva, tongue, palms, oral mucosa and nails; pale palm and sole creases mark severe pallor.

viva.q: What laboratory values match visible jaundice and cyanosis?
viva.a: Bilirubin above 2 mg per dl for jaundice, reduced haemoglobin above 5 grams per dl for cyanosis.

viva.q: How does central cyanosis differ from peripheral?
viva.a: Central stains mucosa plus limbs; peripheral stains the limbs while mucosa stays pink.

viva.q: What is the grade 2 clubbing sign?
viva.a: Loss of the normal 160 degree nail bed angle with a positive Schamroth window test.

aka: Palpating cervical axillary and epitrochlear nodes
items.summary: Ordered palpation of all node groups with the features to record, examiner positioning, and size and spread rules for significant disease.

blocks.title: Features to record per node
bullets: Note number, site, size, shape, surface, warmth, tenderness, consistency and mobility.
Add whether nodes are matted or discrete, any discharge, overlying skin changes, and the drainage area.

blocks.title: Groups to palpate on both sides
bullets: Cover submental, submandibular, cervical front and back, suboccipital, pre and post auricular, axillary, epitrochlear and inguinal groups.
Axillary palpation checks apical, anterior, posterior, medial and lateral sets.

blocks.title: Ordered technique
bullets: For neck nodes stand behind the child for submental, submandibular, preauricular, tonsillar, supraclavicular and deep cervical glands of the front triangle.
Then examine from the front for the back triangle up to the nape, postauricular and occipital nodes.
For the axilla sit facing the child, support the arm, and feel the right side with the left hand and reverse.
For the epitrochlear node hold the partly bent elbow in one hand, steady the wrist with the other, and feel with the thumb; use the left thumb for the left side.

blocks.title: Spread and significance rules
bullets: Disease in one region is localised; two or more separate regions is generalised.
Nodes lasting over 3 months count as persistent.
Significant nodes exceed 1 cm in neck, axilla and elsewhere; groin nodes over 1.5 cm, and an epitrochlear node of any size.

viva.q: How do you position yourself for cervical nodes?
viva.a: Stand behind for the anterior triangle groups, then face the child for the posterior triangle, postauricular and occipital nodes.

viva.q: How is the epitrochlear node felt?
viva.a: Support the wrist with one hand, cradle the partly flexed elbow with the other, and palpate with the thumb of that hand.

viva.q: What counts as significant lymphadenopathy?
viva.a: Over 1 cm in cervical, axillary and other sites, over 1.5 cm in the groin, or any palpable epitrochlear node.

items.summary: Pressing technique for pitting, generalised against localised swelling, and which diseases each distribution suggests.

blocks.title: Pressing technique
bullets: Press over the medial malleolus, shin or foot dorsum with thumb or index finger for 5 seconds.
Record pitting against non pitting, and generalised against localised spread.

blocks.title: Distribution pointers
bullets: Foot swelling points toward cardiac disease and eyelid puffiness toward renal disease.
Ascites points toward liver disease and whole body swelling toward nephrotic syndrome.
Non pitting swelling reflects lymphatic blockage, for example Milroy or Turner syndrome.

viva.q: How do you test for pitting oedema?
viva.a: Press the shin, medial malleolus or foot dorsum firmly for 5 seconds and watch for a pit.

viva.q: What does periorbital versus pedal oedema suggest?
viva.a: Around the eyes favours renal disease; pedal swelling favours cardiac disease.

viva.q: What causes non pitting oedema?
viva.a: Lymphatic obstruction, for example Milroy or Turner syndrome.

title.en: Dehydration grading with ORS and IV plans

aka: WHO Plans A B and C
items.summary: Clinical table separating no, some and severe dehydration with matching feeding, oral rehydration and intravenous fluid plans plus solution composition.

head: Sign
No dehydration
Some dehydration
Severe dehydration
rows: Too thirsty to drink or unable to drink.
Warm limbs with normal pulse, breathing and pressure.
Warm limbs with fast pulse, slow breathing and low pressure.
Cold clammy limbs with rapid feeble pulse, deep sighing breaths and unrecordable pressure.

blocks.title: Plan A for no dehydration
bullets: Keep feeding as usual with continued breast feeds plus World Health Organization oral rehydration salts.
Give 50-100 ml per loose stool below 2 years, 100-200 ml from 2 to 10 years, and free intake above 10 years.
By weight the rule is 10 ml per kg per stool episode.

blocks.title: Plan B for some dehydration
bullets: Keep usual feeding and breast feeds and give 75 ml per kg of oral salts over the first 4 hours.
Reassess at 4 hours: no dehydration moves to Plan A, persisting signs repeat Plan B.

blocks.title: Plan C for severe dehydration
bullets: Start intravenous fluid at once with Ringer lactate plus 5 percent dextrose.
Below 1 year give 30 ml per kg in the first hour, then 70 ml per kg over 5 hours.
From 1 to 5 years give 30 ml per kg in the first half hour, then 70 ml per kg over 2 and a half hours.

head: Content per litre
Older salts mmol per L
New low osmolarity salts mmol per L

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Mixed solution must be used within 24 hours; sachets come for 1 litre or 200 ml.
Give zinc to every child: 10 mg daily below 6 months and 20 mg daily above, once daily for 14 days.
A 5 ml spoon of syrup carries 20 mg of zinc.
Skin pinch means nothing in marasmus, kwashiorkor or obesity.

viva.q: How do pulse and skin pinch differ between some and severe dehydration?
viva.a: Some dehydration shows a fast pulse with slow skin return; severe shows a rapid feeble pulse with very slow return.

viva.q: What is the Plan B oral fluid prescription?
viva.a: 75 ml per kg of oral rehydration salts over the first 4 hours with continued feeding, then reassess.

viva.q: How does new low osmolarity ORS differ from older salts?
viva.a: Sodium falls from 90 to 75, chloride 80 to 65, glucose 111 to 75, and total osmolarity 311 to 245.

viva.q: What zinc dose follows diarrhoea?
viva.a: 10 mg daily below 6 months and 20 mg daily above, once daily for 14 days.

items.summary: Sign by sign table linking each vitamin and trace mineral deficit to the clinical clues the examiner must seek.

head: Nutrient
Bedside clues
rows: Bitot spots, dry eye, corneal softening and toad like goose skin.
Dry beriberi with nerve signs, drooping lids and sluggish reflexes; wet beriberi with palpitation, breathlessness, big heart and swelling.
Red sore tongue, cracked mouth corners and scaly skin.
The three Ds: loose stools, skin rash and memory loss.
Pale small red cells anaemia with poor growth.
Large red cell anaemia with low platelets.
Large red cell anaemia with low platelets, sore tongue and weak immunity.
Scurvy with irritability, false paralysis from pain, beaded ribs, bleeding gums pattern and slow healing.
Rickets with skull bossing, soft skull, late fontanelle closure, beaded ribs, Harrison sulcus, knock knees, bowed shin variant, pot belly and stunting.

head: Mineral
Bedside clues
rows: Soil eating habit, tiredness, irritability, poor effort tolerance, breathlessness on exertion, with slow growth, pallor and spoon nails.
Tetany with hand and foot spasms, cramps, weakness, rickets, stunting and a long QT pattern on the tracing.
Goitre with stunting, slow motor milestones, poor learning, deafness, rough skin, cold intolerance and constipation.
Stunting with limb rash, mouth and skin ulcers, poor healing, small gonads, repeated infection and weak immunity.

viva.q: How do dry and wet beriberi differ?
viva.a: Dry beriberi shows nerve signs with drooping lids and sluggish reflexes; wet adds palpitation, breathlessness, cardiac enlargement and swelling.

viva.q: List four skeletal clues of rickets from the book.
viva.a: Skull bossing, soft skull bones, beaded ribs and Harrison sulcus, plus knock knees and late fontanelle closure.

viva.q: What bedside clues point to iron deficiency?
viva.a: Soil eating, fatigue, irritability, exertional breathlessness, pallor and spoon shaped nails with impaired growth.

viva.q: What are the three Ds of niacin lack?
viva.a: Diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia.

title.en: Face, ear, neck and palate dysmorphism screen

aka: Wide set eyes and low set ears
Delayed dentition and short neck checks
items.summary: Stepwise screen of eye spacing, ear position and pull, hairline, teeth, neck length, nipple spacing, palate height and corneal size with syndrome pointers.

blocks.title: Eye spacing ratios
bullets: Suspect wide spacing when the gap between inner eye corners exceeds one eye width; confirm with a clear sheet.
Wide spacing means the inner to outer corner ratio tops 0.38, seen in Down, Turner, Apert and Noonan syndromes.
Narrow spacing means the same ratio falls below 0.33.

blocks.title: Ear examination and position
bullets: In newborns and infants draw the pinna down and outward with thumb and finger.
In older children draw it up and back.
Ears sit low when under one third rises above a line joining the outer eye corners.
Low ears occur in Down, Marfan, fragile X, Noonan and trisomy 13 and 18 syndromes.

blocks.title: Hairline, teeth, neck and nipples
bullets: A back hairline dipping below the fourth cervical spine is low, as in Turner syndrome.
No teeth by 13 months is delayed, seen in constitutional delay, low thyroid, low pituitary function, rickets and undernutrition.
A neck shorter than one thirteenth of height is short; measure from outer occipital bump to the seventh cervical spine.
Short necks occur in Down, Noonan, trisomy 13 and 18 and low thyroid states.
Nipples spaced wider than a quarter of chest girth suggest Turner syndrome.

blocks.title: Palate and cornea
bullets: The palate arches high when its roof stays hidden with examiner eyes level with the child upper front teeth and mouth open.
Cornea above 13 mm is megalocornea and below 10 mm is microcornea.

viva.q: How do you test for wide set eyes at the bedside?
viva.a: Suspect it when the inner corner gap exceeds one eye width, then confirm the inner to outer corner ratio above 0.38 with a transparent sheet.

viva.q: How does ear pull differ in infants and older children?
viva.a: Pull down and outward in newborns and infants, up and backward in older children.

viva.q: What defines a short neck and delayed dentition here?
viva.a: Neck under one thirteenth of height, and no teeth by 13 months.

unsure: Book also quotes an inner canthal to inner pupillary distance ratio above 0.6 without defining the pairing; left out as ambiguous.

title.en: Limbs, digits, eyes and fontanelle pointers

aka: Knock knees and bow legs testing
items.summary: Knee alignment testing, digit counts and hypermobility signs, eye clues and fontanelle timing that complete the bedside dysmorphism screen.

blocks.title: Knee alignment
bullets: For knock knees stand the child with inner knee bumps touching; a gap over 5 cm between ankle bumps is abnormal.
For bow legs stand the child with inner ankle bumps touching; a gap over 5 cm between knee bumps is abnormal.
Congenital causes and rickets top both lists, with achondroplasia added for bow legs.
Both patterns are normal physiology up to 2 years of age.

blocks.title: Fontanelle timing
bullets: Late closure follows rickets, low thyroid, undernutrition, hydrocephalus and trisomy 13, 18 and 21.
Early closure follows premature suture fusion.

blocks.title: Digits and stretch signs
bullets: Extra digits near thumb or big toe are preaxial; near little finger they are postaxial.
For the thumb sign the child grips the thumb inside the fist; the tip crossing the palm edge suggests Marfan syndrome.
For the wrist sign the child rings one wrist with thumb and little finger of the same side; overlap is positive.

blocks.title: Eye clues
bullets: Blue sclera occurs in brittle bone disease, glaucoma and Marfan syndrome.
Forward bulging eyes occur in retinoblastoma, thyrotoxicosis and orbital cellulitis.
Drooping lids occur in Turner, Noonan and Horner syndromes.

viva.q: How do you test knock knees versus bow legs?
viva.a: Knees together tests knock knees by the ankle gap; ankles together tests bow legs by the knee gap, with 5 cm abnormal in both.

viva.q: How do you elicit the thumb and wrist signs?
viva.a: Grip the thumb inside a fist and watch for tip protrusion past the palm; ring the wrist with same side thumb and little finger and watch for overlap.

viva.q: What does blue sclera suggest?
viva.a: Brittle bone disease first, plus glaucoma and Marfan syndrome.
